paper.title_en: Decoding quantum noise to achieve fault-tolerant computing and advanced error correction
paper.abstract_en: This paper evaluates the scaling requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) through the lens of advanced quantum error correction (QEC) protocols. While current physical two-qubit gate error rates operate near $10^{-3}$, practical quantum utility demands logical error rates suppressed below $10^{-12}$. This discrepancy necessitates a massive resource overhead, historically requiring 1,000 physical qubits per logical qubit in standard surface code architectures. The fundamental novelty of this work lies in establishing a unified vertical co-design framework that bridges theoretical topological bounds directly with empirical microarchitectural constraints, including cryogenic cooling budgets at 15 mK, through-silicon via (TSV) parasitics, and real-time classical decoding latency. In this review and roadmap, we analyze novel decoding algorithms capable of reducing physical qubit overhead by up to 40% under standard circuit-level depolarizing noise models ($p = 10^{-3}$), and evaluate dynamic error mitigation strategies that demonstrate an empirical 3$\times$ improvement in circuit fidelity for shallow-to-intermediate depth benchmarks ($d \le 60$) prior to reaching the fault-tolerant break-even frontier. By projecting a hardware trajectory toward the sub-$10^{-4}$ physical error rate threshold, we systematically outline the microarchitectural, thermodynamic, and software co-design constraints required to synthesize a fully operational, 100-logical-qubit fault-tolerant processor.
